summary: Defines a method for negotiating and using Numbered-Mode, as defined by ISO 7776, to provide a reliable serial link for PPP. It is a standards-track proposal.

eli5.summary: A way to make sure every message on a line arrives, by numbering them and checking.

questions: how does ppp reliable transmission work
what is the ppp numbered-mode option
subtitle: How PPP can switch a serial link from best-effort frames to numbered, acknowledged ones.

tldr.problem: PPP normally sends connectionless datagrams that may be lost, but some uses, such as a compressed link whose dictionary is rebuilt from the data stream, cannot afford to lose a datagram.
tldr.mechanism: A new LCP Numbered-Mode Configuration Option negotiates a window size and an HDLC address, after which the link uses ISO 7776 LAPB numbered frames that are acknowledged and retransmitted.
tldr.outcome: Links that agree get reliable delivery; if the peers disagree, PPP falls back to its default Unnumbered-Information mode. The ISO Multi-Link Procedure it mentions is deprecated in favour of PPP multilink.

today: RFC 1663 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 1661 and RFC 1662, and its own text deprecates the ISO Multi-Link Procedure in favour of PPP multilink.

sections.title: Why Reliability on a Serial Link
sections.content:
By default, PPP packets over HDLC framed links are connectionless datagrams. Datagram networks presume best-effort, non-sequential delivery, so when an error is detected the datagram is simply discarded. Generally, link reliability is not a major issue.

There are cases where a reliable link is advisable. The most obvious is a compressed link: the compression dictionary is recovered from the compressed data stream, so a lost datagram corrupts it. Not every compression type needs this, since the cost of detecting and resetting a corrupt dictionary can be small.

The RFC uses ISO 7776 LAPB to guarantee delivery and calls this Numbered Mode, to distinguish it from the Unnumbered Information used in standard PPP framing. If reliable transmission is wanted, the implementation MUST specify the Numbered-Mode Configuration Option during Link Establishment.
sections.eli5: Most of the time it is fine if a message is lost, like a flyer in a mailbox. But some messages build on each other, so every one has to arrive.

sections.title: Numbered-Mode Frames
sections.content:
Numbered-Mode affects only the Address and Control fields. The Address field MUST take the value announced in the Numbered-Mode Configuration Option, and the Control field MAY take any value valid in ISO 7776. The rest of the frame follows the framing already in use for PPP.

Once the link enters Numbered-Mode, Numbered-Mode MUST be used on all frames, because some implementations cannot cope with Unnumbered-Information control fields or the All-Stations address mixed in with numbered frames.

The frame carries a Flag, a 1 to 2 octet Address, a 1 to 2 octet Control field, a 1 to 2 octet Protocol field, Information, Padding, a 16-bit FCS and a closing Flag. The Protocol, Information and Padding fields come from the PPP encapsulation RFC, and the FCS and Flag come from the PPP in HDLC Framing RFC.
sections.eli5: Only the address label and the control stamp on the envelope change. Once you start using numbered envelopes, you must use them for everything.

sections.title: The Numbered-Mode Configuration Option
sections.content:
The LCP Numbered-Mode Configuration Option negotiates use of Numbered-Mode. By default, or on ultimate disagreement, Unnumbered-Mode is used. The option has Type 11, a Length of at least 4, a Window and an Address.

Window is a value from 1 to 127 giving the number of frames the receiver will buffer, which is the most the sender should send without an acknowledgement. If the window is below 8, modulo 8 sequencing is used; otherwise modulo 128. The two sides may announce different windows, but both must use the same modulus, so a Configure-Nak may reduce the window but may not increase it.

Address is an HDLC address per ISO 3309. ISO 7776 specifies 1 and 3 for single link operation and 7 and 15 for the Multi-Link Procedure. If an address of zero is received, the receiver MUST Configure-Nak with an appropriate one. If both peers send zero, the side with the numerically smaller window picks the smaller address; with equal windows a random choice MUST be made. If magic numbers were negotiated, the system with the smaller magic number SHOULD choose the smaller address.
sections.eli5: The two computers agree how many unanswered messages may be in flight and which 'name tag' each will use. If they cannot agree, they just go back to the plain way.

sections.title: How Numbered-Mode Starts and Ends
sections.content:
The Numbered-Mode option is negotiated, the Magic-Number option MUST also be negotiated, and Address-and-Control-Field-Compression MUST NOT be negotiated. After a successful negotiation the system with the numerically smaller Magic-Number sends a SABM or SABM(E) and the other answers with a UA. If either is lost the exchange can be repeated using the Restart Timer and counter values. Authentication, Link Quality Determination and NCP Configuration follow.

Any later re-negotiation MUST also be conducted in Numbered-Mode. If the option is not successfully re-negotiated, the link reverts to Unnumbered-Information operation before those later phases.

A Numbered-Mode-capable implementation that is not in that mode and sees a frame with a correct FCS but no UI control octet MUST send a DM message, immediately followed by an LCP Configure-Request. An implementation that is in Numbered-Mode and receives a DM MUST revert to Unnumbered-Information operation and immediately send a Configure-Request.
sections.eli5: One side says 'ready?' and the other says 'ready!'. If one side gets confused, it says 'let us start over the simple way'.

sections.title: Single Link, Inverse Multiplexing and Multi-Link
sections.content:
On a single link, network-layer packets pass through header compression, then data compression, then the Numbered Mode header, and out to the link.

Sending packets from one connection over several parallel links is called inverse multiplexing. By default PPP does nothing special: each link is set up and torn down independently and may have different options, which allows dissimilar media such as 56K sync with async backup. Every link in one machine MUST have a different Magic Number, and each end of each link SHOULD use numbers unique to those peers, which guards against patch-panel errors as well as looped-back links. Where compression such as Van Jacobsen relies on sequential delivery and there is no Multi-Link support, it MUST be applied link by link.

The ISO 7776 Multi-Link Procedure MAY be used to restore order across asynchronous parallel links, but its implementation is deprecated and the PPP multilink procedure is recommended instead. The RFC offers no standard for ISO Multi-Link, only a way to agree on addressing for it.
sections.eli5: With one road, trucks arrive in order. With two roads, trucks can arrive mixed up, so you need either numbers on the trucks or to keep each kind of cargo on one road.

sections.title: LAPB Parameter Defaults
sections.content:
Timer T1 is the longest wait before retransmitting after no response to an I frame. It must exceed the time for a maximum-sized frame to arrive and a response to be generated. It SHOULD be set dynamically from the measured round trip time at the LAPB level. If that cannot be measured, it SHOULD be twice the bit rate divided by the maximum bits per frame, plus 100 milliseconds of processing time. The RFC's example is a 14,400 bps link with 8000-bit frames, giving 3.7 seconds.

Timer T3 indicates an idle link and must be greater than T1. N2 is the maximum number of retransmission attempts for a frame; if it is exceeded the link SHOULD be terminated, and the default SHOULD be 3.
sections.eli5: You wait a little while for a 'got it' before sending again, and after three tries you give up on the line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. It notes that Authentication follows the Numbered-Mode setup, but defines no security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: This RFC is about making sure messages arrive, not about keeping them secret.
